objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain safe taxi operations, airport references, signs, markings, lights, wind indicators and aircraft lighting at commercial depth, and teach a learner to control the airplane on the ground, set the controls for the wind, read the airport and handle route changes, while you spot and fix the errors learners make.
why: The AFH names the flight instructor as the key to the formal teaching of safe taxi practices [[24:34|AFH 1-13]]. Taxi habits are set in the first few lessons and then repeated on every flight for a whole career. This lesson is about the airplane on the ground and the airport around it; runway incursion avoidance itself is taught in depth in AI.II.C.

prereading.what: Ramp operations, hand signals, taxi speed, steering, brake check, wind control positions, taxi instrument checks and the run-up.
prereading.label: AFH 2-14 to 2-22

prereading.what: Night taxi and run-up, and tailwheel taxi technique, including elevator position in a tailwind.
prereading.label: AFH 11-7 to 14-3

prereading.what: Airport data sources, hold markings, sign types, taxiway lights and wind direction indicators.
prereading.label: PHAK 14-3 to 14-20

prereading.what: Taxiway lights, marking colors, taxiway markings, nonmovement boundary, closed surfaces and the six sign types.
prereading.label: AIM 2-1-10 to 2-3-13

prereading.what: Wind and landing direction indicators, light gun signals, ground communications, taxi phraseology, low visibility taxi and use of aircraft lights.
prereading.label: AIM 4-3-4 to 4-3-24

prereading.what: Taxi planning, briefing items, situational awareness and exterior lighting for single-pilot operations.
prereading.label: AC 91-73B 7b to 7h

prereading.what: Knowledge of results, learning tasks in isolation, following the learner's eyes, interference and mnemonics, models as aids, and a positive first taxi lesson.
prereading.label: AIH 3-25 to 8-3

warmup: Think first: your new learner has 1.5 hours in the logbook. Today the wind is 15 knots, quartering from behind on the way out to the runway, the ramp is busy with fuel trucks, and the field has a hot spot near the run-up area. You can only teach a few things well on this taxi. What will you teach today, what will you do yourself, and what will you leave for a later lesson? Why?

key_terms.def: Runways, taxiways and other areas under ATC control. While the tower is operating, approval is needed before an aircraft moves onto it.
Two yellow lines, one solid and one dashed. The solid line is on the nonmovement side, the dashed line on the movement side.
A speed slow enough that closing the throttle stops the airplane promptly, so the brakes are not the speed control.
A test of each brake as soon as the airplane starts to move. If braking is unsatisfactory, the engine is shut down at once.
The tendency of the airplane to turn into the wind on the ground. Stronger in tailwheel airplanes and in a direct crosswind.
The aileron on the wing the wind is coming from. Held UP in a quartering headwind and DOWN in a quartering tailwind.
Black background with a yellow inscription and yellow border. Names the taxiway or runway the airplane is on.
Yellow signs with black inscriptions and arrows, read clockwise from the first taxiway on the left, placed before the intersection.
A landing direction indicator. Its small end points in the direction of landing. Not to be used as a wind indicator.
Three steady-burning yellow in-pavement lights at a taxiway holding position, used in low visibility or to show an intersecting taxiway at night.
A pink circle with a black and white ring and a number, left of the centerline on low visibility taxi routes.
An unlighted sign whose legend reflects light back. Often used at airports not certified under Part 139; it shows best in your own taxi or landing light.

chunks.title: K1: Elements of safe taxi operations, and your part in them

body.p: Taxiing is the controlled movement of the airplane under its own power on the surface [[24:55|AFH 2-18]]. The AFH gives three primary requirements for safe taxiing: positive control, the ability to recognize potential hazards in time to avoid them, and the ability to stop or turn where and when desired, without undue reliance on the brakes [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. Use those three as the frame for everything else in this lesson.

head: Element
What to teach
Source
rows: Ramp, parking areas, taxiways, the runway environment, and the people, equipment and aircraft in them. Have the airport diagram out and in view at all times.
If there is any doubt about clearing an object, stop and check. It may be necessary to have the airplane towed or moved by ground crew.
Staying centered on the taxiway centerline does not guarantee wingtip clearance with other aircraft or objects.
Scan from side to side, near and far, to assess the route and potential conflicts.
Exhaust blast or rotor downwash from powerful aircraft can make a light airplane uncontrollable. Consider jet blast, prop wash and rotor wash during all ground operations.
Passengers move on the ramp only as directed, or with an escort if not under the pilot's direct supervision.

body.p: Vigilance belongs to everyone on board. The AFH says both the learner and the instructor need to be continually aware of other aircraft and vehicles on the movement area, and that nontowered airports, where much training happens, call for even more vigilance [[24:34|AFH 1-13]].

callout.text: Frame the first taxi lesson positively. The AIH lists 'if you go too fast, you lose directional control' as a first-lesson message that can turn a new learner off; present the taxi as normal, controlled and learnable [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

check.q: Your learner taxis neatly on the centerline past a parked jet with its wingtip near the taxiway. Why is the centerline alone not enough?
check.a: Being centered on the taxiway centerline does not guarantee wingtip clearance [[33:144|AIM 2-3-4b1]]; if there is any doubt, stop and check the clearance [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

chunks.title: K2: Airport references: Chart Supplement, airport diagram and NOTAMs

body.p: A safe taxi starts at the planning table with current data, not with memory of the last visit. Teach the learner which question each reference answers.

head: Reference
What it gives the taxiing pilot
Source
rows: Issued every 56 days. Holds airport data that cannot be shown on a chart, such as hours of operation, fuel, runway widths and lighting codes, plus airport diagrams. The PHAK calls it the most comprehensive information on a given airport and notes it lists LAHSO airports.
The frequency that turns on pilot-controlled lighting is in the Chart Supplement and the approach charts. It is not on the sectional.

Built to help ground movement at airports with complex runway and taxiway layouts. Not for approach, landing or departure. Helps pilots find their location, which reduces requests for progressive taxi.
Runways with magnetic headings, taxiways, hot spots, nonmovement areas, run-up areas, LAHSO and ILS hold lines, the beacon and lighting.
Time-critical, temporary items, including taxiway and runway closures and construction. Check before every flight.
Weather, runways in use, specific ATC procedures and construction that could affect taxi planning.

body.p: Closures may not be marked on the pavement. Depending on the reason and length of a closure, a visual indication may not be present, so pilots should check NOTAMs and the ATIS for runway and taxiway closures [[33:161|AIM 2-3-6e]].

S2 in the airplane: keep the current diagram available, check the assigned route against it with the heading indicator or compass, and follow progress on it while keeping eyes outside [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7d(1)]]. AI.II.C covers the diagram and hot spot review for incursion avoidance in depth.

callout.text: Recall is promoted by association, and isolated facts tend to be forgotten [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]. Application: instead of reading the Chart Supplement entry aloud, give the learner tomorrow's real airport and three questions: what frequency turns on the lights, when the tower closes, and where the run-up area is.

check.q: Your learner plans a night landing at a nontowered field and looks for the pilot-controlled lighting frequency on the sectional. Where should she look instead?
check.a: In the Chart Supplement or the approach charts; the frequency is not on sectional charts [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8 NOTE]].

body.p: While a tower is operating, approval must be obtained before moving onto the movement area, and the pilot always states the airplane's position on the airport when calling for taxi [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]]. Before departure the request includes the aircraft identification, location, type of operation (VFR or IFR) and point of first intended landing [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18d1]]. After landing, it includes identification, location and the request for taxi [[33:262|AIM 4-3-18d3]].

head: What the learner hears
What it means
Source
rows: Runway, then route, then hold short or crossing

ATC states the runway first, then the route, then any hold short instructions or runway crossings. That does not authorize entering or crossing the departure runway, and ATC does not use the word 'cleared' for taxi.
Taxi to a point other than a runway
ATC names the point, gives the route and states any hold short or crossing instructions.
Always read back the runway assignment, any clearance to enter a specific runway, and any instruction to hold short of a runway or line up and wait.
A taxi clearance is based on known traffic and conditions; avoiding collision stays the pilot's job. Ask for clarification of anything not understood.
Where radio contact cannot be established, a light signal clearance is needed before taxiing on a runway, taking off or landing.

head: Light gun signal to an aircraft on the ground
Meaning
rows: Taxi clear of the runway in use [[33:257|AIM TBL 4-3-1]]
Return to starting point on airport [[33:257|AIM TBL 4-3-1]]

body.p: Acknowledge light signals in daylight by moving the ailerons or rudder, and at night by blinking the landing or navigation lights. If the radio fails after leaving the parking area, watch the tower for light signals or monitor the tower frequency [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13e]]. Writing clearances down and runway crossing procedure are in AI.II.C.

callout.text: Application: write the learner's first three ground calls on a card (initial call, readback, call after landing) using the AIM format, and have the learner say them aloud on the ramp before the engine starts. The card comes out of the airplane as soon as the calls are automatic.

check.q: On a night lesson your learner's radio fails on the ramp. The tower shows a flashing green. How does the learner say 'received'?
check.a: By blinking the landing or navigation lights; flashing green to an aircraft on the ground means cleared for taxi [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13e]] [[33:257|AIM TBL 4-3-1]].

chunks.title: K4: Airport signs: teach them by color and by job

body.p: There are six types of airport signs [[33:161|AIM 2-3-7]]. Teach them as three color families, because the color tells the learner the job before the words are readable.

head: Sign type
Colors
Job
Source
rows: Marks an entrance to a runway or critical area, or an area where aircraft may not enter. Includes runway holding position, approach area, ILS critical area and No Entry signs.
Black background, yellow inscription and yellow border
Names the taxiway or runway you are on.
Names the taxiways leading out of the intersection, with an arrow for each turn.
Yellow background, black inscription, always an arrow
Shows the route to a place such as a runway, FBO apron or fuel.
Areas the tower cannot see, radio frequencies, noise abatement.
Landing runway left, in thousands of feet. The '1' sign is at least 950 feet from the runway end.

body.p: One trap: the runway boundary sign and ILS critical area boundary sign are grouped with location signs, but they are yellow with black inscriptions and a picture of the hold marking. They face the pilot leaving the area and help decide when the airplane is clear [[33:166|AIM 2-3-9a3]] [[33:167|AIM 2-3-9a4]].

bullets: Where to look: signs are normally on the left side of the taxiway as seen by the approaching pilot [[19:44|AC 150/5340-18H 1.13.1]], and direction signs are normally on the left before the intersection [[33:167|AIM 2-3-10c]].

How to read an array: designations run clockwise starting with the first taxiway on the pilot's left. When a location sign is in the array, every left turn is to its left, and straight ahead and right turns are to its right [[33:167|AIM 2-3-10d]] [[33:167|AIM 2-3-10e]].
Nontowered fields may use destination signs instead of direction arrays [[19:16|AC 150/5340-18H 1.3.6]].
Report confusing or wrong signs to the airport operator; they can also go in an Aviation Safety Report [[33:138|AIM 2-3-1c]].

body.p: Teaching it: the AIH says similar material interferes with memory more than different material, and material not well learned suffers most [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]. Location and direction signs are the same two colors reversed, which is exactly that kind of similar material. Put them side by side on purpose, contrast them, and quiz the difference until it is solid. A short mnemonic helps fix it [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

callout.text: Red: stop and ask. Black: where I am. Yellow: where I can go. (A memory aid, not FAA wording.)

check.q: Approaching an intersection, your learner sees a yellow array: '<-E', a black panel 'A', then 'T->' . Which taxiway is she on, and which way is T?
check.a: She is on A, the black location sign; T is a right turn, because right turns sit to the right of the location sign [[33:167|AIM 2-3-10e]] [[33:165|AIM 2-3-9a1]].

chunks.title: K4 and S8: Pavement markings, airport lights and hold lines

body.p: Start with color. Runway markings are white. Taxiway markings, markings for closed and hazardous areas, and holding positions are yellow, even when the holding position is on a runway [[33:138|AIM 2-3-2b]]. Runways have white, segmented centerlines; taxiways have continuous yellow centerlines [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].

head: Marking
What it looks like
What it tells the pilot
Source
rows: Single continuous yellow line, 6 to 12 inches wide
The path to follow; keep the airplane centered on it
Beyond it is shoulder or pavement not meant for aircraft
Broken double yellow lines, 15-foot lines with 25-foot gaps
The pavement beyond it is meant for aircraft, for example an apron
Looks like full-strength pavement but may not support an aircraft
Single dashed yellow line across the taxiway
When told to hold short of that taxiway, no part of the airplane goes beyond it; with no marking, stop with clearance from the crossing traffic
One solid and one dashed yellow line
Solid line on the nonmovement side, dashed on the movement side
Barricades, or a yellow cross at each entrance
Usually treated as a hazardous area that no part of an aircraft may enter
Direction signs beside the centerline; location sign right of it
Left turns are painted on the left of the centerline and right turns on the right

head: Light
What the learner sees
Source
rows: Alternating green and yellow from the runway centerline to one light past the holding position; inside the runway environment or ILS critical area
Three steady yellow in-pavement lights at a taxiway holding position
Pair of flashing yellow elevated lights, or a row of yellow in-pavement lights, at the runway holding position
White and green for a lighted land airport; in daylight in surface areas it often means below 3 miles or a 1,000-foot ceiling, but do not rely on it

body.p: S8, the hold line itself: approaching a runway, stop so that no portion of the airplane intersects the first solid yellow line, and do not cross the solid lines without a clearance [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]]. At an ILS critical area hold, stop only when ATC says to hold short of it [[1:346|PHAK 14-12]]. Clearing the runway after landing, and the whole tail past the dashed side, are taught in AI.II.C.

callout.text: Application: from the left seat the hold line disappears under the cowling well before the nosewheel reaches it. On an early lesson, stop at a hold line on a quiet taxiway, shut down if it is safe and allowed, and let the learner see where the propeller and nosewheel really are.

check.q: Taxiing past an apron, the learner sees broken double yellow edge lines on her left. May aircraft use the pavement beyond them?
check.a: Yes. Dashed edge markings are used where the adjoining pavement is intended for aircraft, such as an apron [[33:145|AIM 2-3-4c2]].

body.p: At a towered airport ATC gives the wind; FSS or a CTAF may also give it. Where none is available, visual indicators show the wind and runway in use. Teach the learner to check them even when wind is given on the CTAF, because there is no assurance that information is accurate [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]].

head: Indicator
How to read it
Caution
Source
rows: The large end points into the wind. It stands out straighter in strong wind and moves back and forth when gusting, so speed and gust can be estimated
Look at it first if there is one: a tee or tetrahedron can be set by hand to the runway in use
The large end (cross bar) points into the wind
Where a sock is next to it, the tee may be set by hand to the runway in use, so look at the sock
A landing direction indicator; the small end points in the direction of landing
Not a wind indicator. In very light or calm wind it may not line up with the calm-wind runway. At a towered field, use it only when the tower is closed
Segmented circle and traffic pattern indicators
Show pattern direction when it differs from left traffic
Indicators may sit near the runway end if there is no circle

body.p: Teaching it: the AIM suggests the pilot mentally enlarge the indicator for the runway in use so the base and final legs become apparent [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4c]]. On the ground, use the same trick for taxiing: have the learner look at the sock, say where the wind is relative to the nose on the next leg, and only then set the controls. At night wind is harder to detect, so it needs more attention in planning [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

check.q: At a field with a wind tee beside a wind sock, the tee points to Runway 18 but the sock stands out from the west. Which tells the wind?
check.a: The sock. A wind tee next to a sock may be manually aligned with the runway in use [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b2]] [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]].

chunks.title: S3: Teaching control positions for the wind

body.p: In no wind, at normal taxi speed, the ailerons and elevator do little for directional control. They are not steering devices and stay neutral [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. When there is wind, they are positioned to keep it from lifting a wing or the tail.

head: Wind
Ailerons
Elevator, nosewheel airplane
Tailwheel note
Source
rows: Upwind aileron UP (yoke toward the wind). The downwind aileron goes down, adding a little lift and drag on that wing
Full aft to hold the tail down, closer to neutral if the headwind gets very strong
Upwind aileron DOWN (yoke away from the wind)
DOWN (yoke forward), so the wind cannot get under the tail and wing
Stick forward is essential in strong tailwinds; in light winds the propeller wash may give a net headwind over the tail, so sample the wind
Normally only rudder pressure is needed in a nosewheel airplane
Weathervaning is greatest in a direct crosswind; brakes may be needed

body.p: Brief the turns. Swerves are most likely when turning from a downwind heading toward an upwind heading, and in moderate to high wind the airplane may weathervane, adding to the swerve [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. Slow down before those turns.

How to teach it: start with a model. A model that can be moved helps explain how parts work together, especially in a small discussion where the learner asks questions [[25:130|AIH 5-27]]. Hold a model airplane on the table, point a pen at it as the wind, and have the learner move the model's ailerons and elevator for each quadrant. In the airplane, demonstrate one leg while saying 'wind from the left rear, yoke right and forward,' then have the learner call and set each new leg before the turn is finished.

callout.text: Headwind: yoke into it. Tailwind: yoke forward and away from it. (A memory aid, not FAA wording.)

Watch for the learner who turns the yoke in every taxi turn as if steering a car. That is the 'ailerons are not steering devices' error [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]; fix it on the first lesson before it becomes a habit.

check.q: Wind 240 at 15 knots. On heading 270 the learner correctly holds the yoke left with the elevator neutral. She turns to 090 and leaves the yoke where it was. What should it be now?
check.a: The wind is now 150 degrees right of the nose, a right rear quartering tailwind: upwind (right) aileron down, so the yoke stays left, and elevator down, so the yoke goes forward [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

chunks.title: S5 and S6: Positive control: speed, steering and brakes

bullets: Starting: more power may be needed to start moving or start a turn; retard the throttle as soon as the airplane moves to prevent excess speed [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

Brake check (S5): as soon as the airplane moves, retard the throttle and press just enough on one brake, then the other. If braking is unsatisfactory, shut down the engine immediately [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].
Speed (S6): slow enough that closing the throttle stops the airplane promptly; cautious on busy ramps [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

Steering: rudder in the direction of turn, held until just short of the point where the turn stops; brake only to tighten a turn after full pedal. Some models have no nosewheel steering and steer with brakes [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].
Turns: slow down first. Sharp, fast turns side-load the gear and can cause tire damage, a swerve or a ground loop [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].
Downwind: keep power to a minimum and brake only occasionally. Except in sharp turns at low speed, the throttle is at idle before the brakes are used [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].
Stopping: stop with the nosewheel straight to relieve side load and make it easier to start [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

Tracking: put the yellow centerline under the center of the fuselage; signs and lights beside the taxiway can hit the airplane or propeller [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. Taxiway design assumes cockpit-over-centerline steering [[20:71|AC 150/5340-1M 4.2.3.1]].

head: Tailwheel difference
What to teach
Source
rows: Rudder to start the turn, neutralize as it continues, opposite rudder to stop it. The most important tailwheel lesson is to taxi and turn slowly
Heels on the floor, balls of the feet on the rudder pedals; slide up to the brakes only when needed
Start slowly, retard the throttle and apply both brakes smoothly; shut down if braking is poor
Start every move with a small turn and taxi in slow S-turns
Damage comes from rudder held too long, not from too much rudder

body.p: How to teach it: before learners combine tasks, they should be able to do each one reasonably well in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. On the first taxi lessons, you handle the radio and the diagram while the learner only steers, brakes and manages speed in a quiet area; add the other tasks one at a time. Tell learners promptly when they are right or wrong and do not let them practice a mistake, because unlearning is harder than learning it right the first time [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]. Brake riding is the classic one.

callout.text: Teaching risk (application): a learner who gets behind on speed often pushes the pedals harder, which may add rudder instead of brake. Brief before the flight who will stop the airplane, and how, if you say 'I have the flight controls' on the ground.

check.q: Your learner's first brake application is at the run-up area, 600 feet from the tie-down. What did she skip, and what is the AFH standard?
check.a: The brake check, done as soon as the airplane is put in motion: throttle back and a little pressure on one side, then the other; shut down if braking is poor [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

chunks.title: K7a, K7b and K7c: before you move, on the radio, at the runway

body.p: K7 lists five procedures. AI.II.C teaches them in depth for runway incursion avoidance; here is what you teach and check on every taxi.

head: Procedure
What to teach
Source
rows: Appropriate flight deck activities prior to taxi, route planning and Hot Spots (K7a)

Review NOTAMs, ATIS, the current diagram and hot spots; brief the expected route, hold short lines, runways to cross and hot spots; set flaps, trim and GPS entries before the first move. A hot spot is a brown circle or ellipse labeled like 'HS 1' on the diagram

Call ground or clearance delivery before starting the engine; stay on ground through taxi and run-up, then change to tower when ready. Most ground frequencies are 121.6 to 121.9. After landing, stay with tower until told to change

Announce before taxiing and before taxiing onto the runway for departure. UNICOM on the published CTAF; with no tower, FSS or UNICOM, self-announce on MULTICOM 122.9. Two-way radio is not required but is good practice

Towered: an explicit clearance for every crossing. Nontowered: only when the runway is clear and no aircraft is on final, with extreme caution, looking both ways. Scan the full length and the final approach first; all exterior lights on; cross in a timely manner

body.p: S4, checklists: do any taxi checklist items the POH requires. If there are none, taxiing is still the time to check the flight instruments: airspeed at or near zero (depending on taxi speed and wind), attitude level with no flags, altimeter at field elevation within limits, turn indicator showing the correct direction with the ball to the outside, heading indicator set and checked against the compass, and VSI at zero [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Run checklists only when stopped or taxiing straight with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]].

Run-up: pick firm ground free of debris, clear of other aircraft and the taxiway, with nothing behind that the propeller blast could damage. Roll forward a little to line up the nosewheel or tailwheel, and split attention between inside and outside, because a slipping brake can let the airplane move unnoticed [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

callout.text: Application: grade K7a at the tie-down. If the learner cannot point to the hot spots and the hold lines on the route before engine start, the engine does not start yet.

check.q: Taxiing in a calm wind, the learner reports 12 knots on the airspeed indicator. Does that fail the taxi instrument check?
check.a: Not by itself. The AFH says airspeed should be at or near zero depending on taxi speed, wind and the indicator's low-end sensitivity [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]; compare it with the taxi speed and wind before calling it a fault.

chunks.title: K6, K7d and K7e: aircraft lights, night taxi and low visibility

callout.text: From sunset to sunrise no one may operate an aircraft without lighted position lights. An aircraft with an anticollision light system must have it on, unless the PIC decides that turning it off is in the interest of safety because of operating conditions [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]].

head: Aircraft lighting (K6): moment
Lights
Source
rows: Rotating beacon on. The beacon program is voluntary, so never assume an engine is off just because its beacon is off
Navigation, position and anticollision lights. Taxi light on while moving or about to move, off when stopped or yielding. No strobes if they would affect other pilots or ground crew
All exterior lights, within equipment limits
Entering for takeoff or line up and wait
All lights except landing lights; landing lights on with takeoff clearance, or at the start of the roll at a nontowered field
Calling the tower at night with no radio
Landing light on, airplane placed clear of the active runway where the tower can see the light

body.p: Night taxi operations (K7d): check every light by turning it on during preflight, and tap the position light fixtures to find loose connections. Check the ramp with a flashlight, take extra care clearing the propeller area, and taxi slowly; some landing lights overheat or drain the battery if left on. Confirm that position, route and runway all look as expected, and do not continue if anything conflicts [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]. At airports not certified under Part 139, signs may be unlighted with retroreflective legends, and lighted signs are more visible at a distance than retroreflective ones [[19:16|AC 150/5340-18H 1.3.10]]. Application: teach the learner that at a small field at night, a sign may only appear when the taxi light hits it.

Low visibility taxi operations (K7e): in some conditions the tower cannot see the airplane, so it cannot confirm the pilot is following instructions. Tell the controller at the first sign of disorientation, use extreme caution taxiing toward the sun, and hold checklists and nonessential talk until stopped with the brakes set [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19]]. On low visibility routes (below 1,200 feet RVR), pink geographic position markings with numbers sit left of the centerline [[33:149|AIM 2-3-4g]]. Steady green centerline lights guide the taxi [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10b]]. Never cross a lit red stop bar even if cleared, and if the lead-on lights go out after crossing one, hold position and call ATC [[33:134|AIM 2-1-10e]].

callout.text: Teaching risk: the first night taxi should be at the home airport the learner already knows by day. Isolated skills first, then combinations [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

check.q: In fog after crossing a stop bar, the green lead-on lights ahead of your learner suddenly go dark. What now?
check.a: Hold position and contact ATC for further instructions [[33:134|AIM 2-1-10e NOTE]].

chunks.title: R1, R2 and R4: distractions, bias and runway incursion from the right seat

body.p: AI.II.C teaches these three risks in depth. For this Task, add how they show up while the learner is still learning to control the airplane on the ground.

head: Risk
How it shows up in taxi training
Your mitigation
Source
rows: A distraction pulls attention away; when a task is put off, it is easy to forget it entirely
Limit your own instruction while taxiing; phones and devices off; split run-up attention inside and outside
A pilot used to the same clearance hears the expected route, not the one given; confirmation bias suppresses what does not fit
Follow the clearance actually received; on the ground you can always stop and resume
Any incorrect presence on the protected area of a surface for landing and takeoff. About 65 percent are caused by pilots, almost half of those GA pilots
If unsure of position, never stop on a runway; stop and advise ATC

body.p: Spotting the problem: follow where the learner looks. A learner who stares at one thing too long may be fixating; one whose gaze never goes to an area may be inattentive. Looking in a direction is not the same as seeing, so ask what they see [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. On the ground that means eyes on the nose instead of scanning near and far, or eyes in the lap on the diagram while rolling.

check.q: During taxi your learner's eyes stay on the yellow line just ahead of the nose. What AIH problem may this be, and what do you do?
check.a: Possible fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]; teach the AFH scan from side to side, near and far [[24:56|AFH 2-19]], and ask what she sees ahead.

chunks.title: R3: A taxi route or departure runway change

body.p: Planning sets expectations, and the hazard is following the plan instead of the new instruction. Once instructions are received the route is reviewed and monitored, and any change to the taxi route must be fully understood [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(d)]] [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(e) CAUTION]].

head: What changed
What the learner redoes
Source
rows: Write the new instructions, read back the runway and any hold short, and retrace the route on the diagram, looking again for hot spots near it
A route onto a surface the NOTAM or ATIS says is closed
Reset the heading bug and confirm heading and runway agree before adding power; give the takeoff briefing again out loud, including a visual check of the correct surface

Work out any new takeoff data only while stopped: AC 91-73B lists calculating takeoff data with the heads-down tasks done stopped. Application: a new runway can mean a new length and wind, so recheck the takeoff distance
The wind relative to the route
Stop, then ask for progressive taxi; do heads-down work only while stopped

body.p: Teaching it: build the change into a scenario. A good scenario has clear objectives, fits the learner's needs and uses the local environment [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Application: after a few lessons on the usual route, ask ground (traffic permitting) for the other runway, or simply say 'Ground just changed us to Runway 9' while stopped, and watch whether the learner redoes the bug, briefing and route or just turns.

callout.text: A change heard while moving near a hot spot is a reason to stop first. If anything about position, route or runway conflicts, do not continue the taxi or the takeoff [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

check.q: Ground changes your learner from Runway 27 to Runway 9 halfway to the run-up. She reads it back and keeps taxiing. Name two things she has not redone yet.
check.a: Any two of: retrace the new route and hot spots on the diagram [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7g(1)]], reset the heading bug [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]], redo the takeoff briefing with a visual check of the surface [[24:59|AFH 2-22]], and reset control positions for the new wind angle [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

body.p: On the practical test the skill elements read 'demonstrates and simultaneously explains how to' (ACS AI.V.D Skills). The evaluator may also play a learner so you can analyze and correct simulated errors (ACS Appendix 1). Plan your taxi demonstration as a talk-through.

head: Stage
What you do
Source
rows: Diagram, today's wind and control positions on a model, route and hot spots, lights. Positive, normal framing
From the right seat, taxi and say each action: brake check, speed by throttle, wind position on each leg, hold line stop
Learner steers, brakes and manages speed in a quiet area; you take the radio and diagram
Learner adds the readback (S1), diagram tracking (S2) and checklists at the right moments (S4)
Follow the learner's eyes; give results right away and do not let a mistake be practiced
Scenarios: night at home, an unfamiliar towered field, a route or runway change

body.p: S7 includes signals. Some ramps have staff who marshal airplanes with hand signals; the AFH shows the common ones and notes that at night the emergency stop signal is used for every stop. What matters most is that everyone uses an agreed-upon set [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]. Teach the learner that the signalman's instruction never replaces the pilot's own clearance from objects [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

bullets: S1: say the readback aloud and point to it on paper.
S2: touch the diagram at each turn: 'we are here, next is Bravo, then the hot spot.'
S3: 'Wind left front, yoke left, elevator neutral.'
S5: 'Throttle back, left brake, right brake, good.'
S6: 'Throttle sets the speed; I am off the brakes.'
S7 and S8: 'Red sign, solid lines on our side: stop with the nose short of the first solid line.'

callout.text: Application: on the checkride, narrate at the learner's level, not the evaluator's. Short sentences, one action each, matched to what your hands and feet are doing.

check.q: The evaluator, playing your learner, taxis with the throttle at 1,500 rpm and rides the brakes. What do you say and show?
check.a: That the throttle, not the brakes, sets taxi speed: retard power once moving, throttle at idle before braking, and taxi slow enough that closing the throttle stops the airplane [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[24:57|AFH 2-20]]. Then demonstrate it.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Power stays up, brakes drag, the nose dips at each stop
Power to start, then retard; idle before braking; speed set by throttle [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[24:57|AFH 2-20]]
Tires scrub, the airplane swerves turning into the wind
Slow down before every turn, most of all from downwind toward upwind [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]
Steering with the ailerons, or no wind correction
Yoke turned in calm-wind turns; yoke neutral in a strong quartering tailwind
Ailerons are not steering devices; reset ailerons and elevator for each new leg [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]
First brake use at the run-up
Check both brakes as soon as the airplane moves; shut down if poor [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]
Wheel tracks drift toward edge lights and signs
Centerline under the center of the fuselage [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]
Eyes in the lap on the diagram or GPS
Heads-down tasks only when stopped; scan side to side, near and far [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]] [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]
Hard to start straight, side load on the nosewheel
Run-up creep or poor run-up spot
Airplane moves during the run-up; gravel behind or ahead
Firm, clean spot, roll forward to align the nosewheel, split attention outside; hold the brakes at night [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]
Spinner or nosewheel across the first solid line
Stop so no portion of the airplane intersects it [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]]
Neutralize the pedals as the turn develops, then opposite rudder to stop it [[24:288|AFH 14-2]] [[24:289|AFH 14-3]]
Heading indicator never compared to the compass
Check the instruments in taxi turns and on straight segments [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]

body.p: When a learner cannot fix an error at taxi speed, stop the airplane. On the ground the pilot can always stop and resume after addressing an issue [[30:47|RMH 6-4]], and a stopped airplane is the best classroom on the airport.

check.q: Your learner's run-up spot puts the tail toward an open hangar door and the nosewheel is cocked 20 degrees. What two things should she fix before running up?
check.a: Nothing should be behind that the propeller blast could damage, and she should roll forward slightly to align the nosewheel with the longitudinal axis [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

f1.caption: Figure 2-15. Control positions of the nosewheel airplane. (AFH 2-20)
f1.alt: Top view of an airplane in a circle split into four colored quadrants, each with a wind arrow. Front quadrants: use up aileron on the wing the wind comes from and neutral elevator. Rear quadrants: use down aileron on the wing the wind comes from and down elevator.

f2.caption: Figure 14-37. Wind direction indicators. (PHAK 14-21)
f2.alt: An airport scene beside Runway 16 with a wind arrow, showing a wind sock or cone on a pole, a tetrahedron and a wind tee, each labeled.

f3.caption: Figure 2-13. Standard hand signals used to assist pilots in managing a safe departure from the ramp to the taxiway or runway. At night, the Emergency Stop signal is used for all stop indications. (AFH 2-15)
f3.alt: Drawings of a signalman showing standard signals: flagman directs pilot to signalman, signalman's position, signalman directs towing, stop, come ahead, emergency stop, cut engines, start engines, pull chocks, insert chocks, slow down, all clear, left turn, right turn and night operation with lighted wands.

f4.caption: FIG 2-3-35. Direction Sign Array with Location Sign on Far Side of Intersection. (AIM 2-3-31)
f4.alt: Diagram of Taxiway A meeting an intersection with Taxiway E going left and right and Taxiways F and T angling ahead left and right. Before the intersection a yellow sign array reads left arrow E, up-left arrow F, a black A location panel, T up-right arrow, E right arrow. A second array without the location panel is shown below it. A black diamond F location sign stands on the far side on Taxiway F. A note says signs are oriented left to right in a clockwise manner.

f5.caption: FIG 2-3-9. Dashed Markings. (AIM 2-3-11)
f5.alt: Two pairs of double yellow lines: on the left a continuous pair labeled taxiway edge markings continuous, on the right a broken pair labeled taxiway edge markings dashed.

f6.caption: FIG 2-1-12. Taxiway Lead-On Light Configuration. (AIM 2-1-11)
f6.alt: Dusk view from a taxiway holding position toward a runway. A yellow taxiway centerline curves onto the runway with alternating green and yellow in-pavement lights along it; a runway holding position marking crosses the taxiway in the foreground.

scenario.title: Gusty first taxi, then a runway change
scenario.setup: Your learner has two hours of dual. The towered home field reports wind 210 at 16 gusting 22. The tie-down faces north; the route to Runway 27 runs south on Alpha, then east on Bravo past a hot spot at the Bravo and Charlie intersection. A fuel truck is working two rows over. Halfway down Bravo, ground changes the runway to 18.

questions.q: What do you brief on the ground before the engine starts?
questions.a: The route, hold lines and the Bravo/Charlie hot spot on the current diagram [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(d)]] [[2:124|Chart Users' Guide, Hot Spots]], the wind and the control position for each leg using a model [[25:130|AIH 5-27]] [[24:56|AFH 2-19]], and who handles the radio today [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

questions.q: Leaving the tie-down, what should the learner do in the first few feet?
questions.a: Retard the throttle once moving and check the brakes, one side then the other; shut down if braking is poor [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

questions.q: Heading south on Alpha (180) with the wind from 210: how should the controls be held?
questions.a: The wind is 30 degrees right of the nose, a quartering headwind: right aileron up (yoke right), elevator neutral in a nosewheel airplane [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

questions.q: Turning east onto Bravo (090), the wind is now 120 degrees right of the nose. What changes, and what turn hazard do you point out?
questions.a: It is a right rear quartering tailwind: right aileron down (yoke left) and elevator down (yoke forward) [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. Later turns from this downwind heading back toward the wind are where swerves are most likely, so slow down first [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

questions.q: Ground changes the runway to 18. What must the learner redo?
questions.a: Read back the new runway and any hold short [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]], retrace the route and hot spots [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7g(1)]], reset the heading bug [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]], redo the takeoff briefing [[24:59|AFH 2-22]] and the wind positions for the new legs [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. If confused, stop and ask [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

questions.q: The learner taxis downwind on Bravo with the brakes dragging. How do you fix it?
questions.a: Minimum power downwind, occasional braking only, throttle at idle before braking [[24:57|AFH 2-20]]. Tell her now and do not let her practice the mistake [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].

skills.do: Receive and correctly read back clearances and instructions, if applicable. The evaluator sees you read back the runway assignment and every hold short or runway entry with the call sign, while explaining to the 'learner' why those items are read back.
skills.practice: Record the ATIS and ground calls at your field and practice readbacks from paper, then teach a friend the AIM readback list [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]].

skills.do: Use an airport diagram or taxi chart during taxi, if published, and maintain situational awareness. You keep the diagram in view, say where you are and what comes next, and point out hot spots before reaching them.
skills.practice: Talk through taxis at an unfamiliar airport on the diagram at home, saying each turn and hold line aloud [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7d(1)]].

skills.do: Position the flight controls for the existing wind, if applicable. You set and reset aileron and elevator for every leg and explain each setting as you make it, then catch and correct a simulated wrong position.
skills.practice: With a model airplane and a list of headings and winds, explain each quadrant until you can do it without the figure [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[25:130|AIH 5-27]].

skills.do: Complete the appropriate checklist(s). You run the POH checklists at the right moments (stopped or straight ahead) and explain the taxi instrument checks.
skills.practice: Write your trainer's taxi instrument check as a flow and teach it on the ground, then in the airplane [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]].

skills.do: Perform a brake check immediately after the airplane begins moving. The evaluator sees the check in the first few feet, with the throttle back, and hears you say what you would do if braking were poor.
skills.practice: Make the check part of your own taxi flow on every flight so your demonstration is automatic [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

skills.do: Maintain positive control of the airplane during ground operations by controlling direction and speed without excessive use of brakes. You taxi at a throttle-dependent speed on the centerline, slow before turns, and explain why the brakes are not the speed control.
skills.practice: Taxi with a CFI watching your feet and the throttle; then coach another applicant who plays a brake-riding learner [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

skills.do: Comply with airport/taxiway markings, signals, and air traffic control (ATC) clearances and instructions. You name each sign, marking and light you pass and do what it requires, including any marshaller's signals.
skills.practice: Walk or drive (with permission) your home airport's signs with the AIM sign list, then teach the color families aloud [[33:161|AIM 2-3-7]] [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

skills.do: Position the airplane properly relative to hold lines. You stop with no part of the airplane past the first solid line, and explain how to judge it from the seat.
skills.practice: Stop at a hold line on a quiet taxiway and check the real nose position from outside the airplane [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]].

quiz.q: According to the AIM, where are taxiway direction signs normally placed?
options: Only on the far side of the intersection
On the right, after the intersection
On the left, before the intersection
In the middle of the intersection
quiz.why: Direction signs are normally located on the left prior to the intersection [[33:167|AIM 2-3-10c]].

quiz.q: Which statement about the runway boundary sign is correct?
options: It is black with a yellow inscription and marks the runway you are on
It is red with a white inscription and requires a clearance to pass
It is only used at nontowered airports
It is yellow with a black inscription and faces the pilot exiting the runway
quiz.why: It has a yellow background, black inscription and a graphic of the hold marking, and faces the runway to help pilots judge when they are clear [[33:166|AIM 2-3-9a3]].

quiz.q: A pair of elevated flashing yellow lights, one on each side of a taxiway, marks:
options: A taxiway/taxiway holding position
A runway holding position (runway guard lights)
The end of the usable taxiway
A temporarily closed taxiway
quiz.why: Runway guard lights are a pair of elevated flashing yellow lights, or a row of in-pavement yellow lights, at the runway holding position marking [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10d]].

quiz.q: Which way does the small end of a tetrahedron point?
options: Toward the calm-wind runway in all conditions
Toward the control tower
In the direction of landing
Into the wind
quiz.why: The small end points in the direction of landing, and it should not be used as a wind indicator [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b3]].

quiz.q: In a tricycle-gear airplane taxiing into a moderate headwind, the elevator should be held:
options: Full forward
Neutral
Full aft
Wherever the trim leaves it
quiz.why: In nosewheel airplanes the elevator is held neutral; full aft is the tailwheel technique [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

quiz.q: Three steady yellow in-pavement lights across a taxiway at a taxiway holding position are:
options: A stop bar
Lead-off lights
Clearance bar lights
Runway guard lights
quiz.why: Clearance bars are three in-pavement steady-burning yellow lights at taxiway holding positions [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10c]].

quiz.q: Under 14 CFR 91.209, when may an anticollision light system be off?
options: Any time during daylight
Only when the system is placarded inoperative
Whenever the airplane is on the ground
When the PIC decides it is in the interest of safety because of operating conditions
quiz.why: The anticollision lights need not be lit when the PIC determines, because of operating conditions, that turning them off is in the interest of safety [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]].

quiz.q: A pink circle with a number, left of the taxiway centerline, marks:
options: A run-up area
A geographic position on a low visibility taxi route
A hot spot
A VOR receiver checkpoint
quiz.why: Geographic position markings identify aircraft location on low visibility routes below 1,200 feet RVR, left of the centerline [[33:149|AIM 2-3-4g]].

quiz.q: Why does the AIH idea of interference matter when you teach location and direction signs?
options: Signs are learned only by repetition, so more repetitions always help
Learners forget signs they do not like
Similar material interferes with memory more than dissimilar material, and the two signs use the same colors reversed
Interference only affects learners over 40
quiz.why: Similar material interferes with memory more than dissimilar material, and poorly learned material suffers most [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].

quiz.q: After a departure runway change, which AFH item helps prevent a wrong-surface takeoff?
options: A second run-up
Turning on the strobes
Switching to the tower frequency early
A takeoff briefing out loud that includes visual verification of the correct surface
quiz.why: The takeoff briefing should include a visual verification of the correct surface and direction [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

final_quiz.q: You teach a night lesson at a small non-Part 139 airport. Your learner says she cannot see the hold sign until the last moment. Which statement from AC 150/5340-18H explains it?
options: Retroreflective signs are brighter than lighted signs
Such airports may use unlighted retroreflective signs, and lighted signs are more visible at a distance
All signs at such airports are lighted, so the bulb must be out
Signs are not required at nontowered airports
final_quiz.why: Non-139 airports may install unlighted retroreflective signs; lighted signs are generally more discernible at a greater distance [[19:16|AC 150/5340-18H 1.3.10]].

final_quiz.q: Heading 240, wind 300 at 18 knots, nosewheel trainer. How should your learner hold the controls?
options: Yoke left and forward
Yoke left, elevator neutral
Yoke right and forward
Yoke right, elevator neutral
final_quiz.why: 300 - 240 = 60 degrees right of the nose, a right quartering headwind: right aileron up (yoke right), elevator neutral [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

final_quiz.q: Heading 120, wind 270 at 15 knots, nosewheel trainer. How should the controls be held?
options: Yoke right, elevator aft
Yoke left, elevator neutral
Yoke right and forward
Yoke left and forward
final_quiz.why: 270 - 120 = 150 degrees right of the nose, a quartering tailwind from the right rear. The upwind (right) aileron goes down, which means yoke to the left, away from the wind, and the elevator goes down, yoke forward [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

final_quiz.q: In a tailwheel airplane with a light quartering tailwind, your learner asks where to hold the stick fore and aft. What does the AFH tailwheel chapter say?
options: Always full forward in any tailwind
Neutral at all times
Forward is essential in strong tailwinds, but in light winds the propeller wash may give a net headwind over the tail, so sample the wind
Always full aft in any wind
final_quiz.why: Stick forward is essential in strong tailwinds, but in light winds prop wash may make back stick more helpful; sample the wind as you taxi [[24:288|AFH 14-2]].

final_quiz.q: A learner pulls out of the tie-down and, 300 feet later at 10 knots, presses both brakes hard to 'check' them. What is the best coaching point?
options: The check is fine as long as it happens before the run-up
Brake checks should be done at full power to be valid
Brake checks are only needed in tailwheel airplanes
Check the brakes as soon as the airplane moves, slowly, with the throttle back, one side then the other
final_quiz.why: The brakes are tested as soon as the airplane is put in motion, with the throttle retarded and pressure on one side then the other [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

final_quiz.q: Before a learner's first taxi, which opening does the AIH warn against?
options: 'If you go too fast, you lose directional control of the aircraft'
'Today we will taxi to the run-up area and back'
'Your feet steer and the throttle sets the speed'
'Ask me anything as we go'
final_quiz.why: The AIH lists that taxi warning as a negative first-lesson message that can discourage a new learner [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

final_quiz.q: On a long downwind taxi your learner keeps 1,200 rpm and holds light brake pressure the whole way. What should she do instead?
options: Keep power to a minimum, brake only occasionally, and close the throttle before braking
Zigzag to slow down
Add power and brake harder to stay in control
Use the parking brake intermittently
final_quiz.why: Downwind taxiing needs minimum power and only occasional braking; the throttle is at idle before braking except in sharp, slow turns [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

final_quiz.q: At night your radio fails while you are on the ramp at a towered airport and you want the tower's attention for a light signal. What does the AIM suggest?
options: Rock the wings
Turn on a landing light and taxi to a spot clear of the active runway where the tower can see it
Flash the strobes while taxiing toward the runway
Taxi onto the runway and wait
final_quiz.why: Between sunset and sunrise, turn on a landing light and taxi clear of the active runway so the light is visible to the tower [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13c]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner stops at a runway hold line. The nosewheel is short of the first solid line, but the spinner is over it. Is that acceptable?
options: Yes, at a nontowered airport
No; no portion of the airplane may intersect the first solid line without a clearance
Yes, if the runway is clear
Yes; only the wheels count
final_quiz.why: The airplane must stop so no portion of it intersects the first solid yellow line [[1:342|PHAK 14-8]].

final_quiz.q: Leaving the FBO ramp at a towered airport, your learner sees a solid yellow line on her side and a dashed line beyond it. What does it mean?
options: It marks the taxiway edge; continue
She is entering a closed area
She is at a runway hold line
She is leaving the nonmovement area; approval is needed before moving onto the movement area
final_quiz.why: The solid line is on the nonmovement side of the boundary marking [[33:159|AIM 2-3-6c]], and approval is needed before moving onto the movement area while the tower operates [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a]].

final_quiz.q: A learner sees a wind tee aligned with Runway 36 and a wind sock beside it standing straight out toward the east. What do you teach?
options: The sock shows the wind from the west; the tee may be set by hand to the runway in use
Use the average of the two
The tee always shows the wind exactly
Both indicate the landing direction only
final_quiz.why: The large end of the sock points into the wind, and a tee next to a sock may be manually aligned with the runway in use [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b2]].

final_quiz.q: Ground changes your learner's departure runway as she reaches a hot spot. What is the best first action?
options: Keep moving and sort it out at the run-up
Stop, then write and read back the new instructions and retrace the route before continuing
Switch to tower for confirmation while taxiing
Read back 'Roger' and turn toward the new runway
final_quiz.why: Changes must be fully understood [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(d)]]; heads-down work belongs to a stopped airplane [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]], and on the ground the pilot can always stop [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

final_quiz.q: In low visibility, ground clears your learner across a runway, but the red stop bar ahead is still lit. What do you teach?
options: Cross; the clearance overrides the lights
Cross only after flashing the landing light
Do not cross a lit red stop bar even with a clearance; stay put and query ATC
Cross if no aircraft is visible on final
final_quiz.why: Pilots should never cross a red illuminated stop bar, even if ATC has cleared them onto or across the runway [[33:134|AIM 2-1-10e CAUTION]]; anything not understood is clarified with the controller [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b]].

takeaways: Safe taxiing is positive control, seeing hazards in time, and stopping or turning where you want without leaning on the brakes.
Teach signs by color family: red means stop and ask, black means where you are, yellow means where you can go.
Wind positions: yoke into a headwind, forward and away from a tailwind; reset them after every turn.
Brake check in the first few feet; throttle, not brakes, sets taxi speed.
A route or runway change means redo the readback, the route on the diagram, the heading bug and the takeoff briefing.
Teach control alone first, then add radio, diagram and checklists one at a time.
Watch the learner's eyes and feet: they show fixation and brake riding before the airplane does.
cfi_notes: The PHAK describes location signs as black with a yellow inscription and says they also identify the boundary of the runway [[1:349|PHAK 14-15]], but the AIM describes the runway boundary sign as yellow with a black inscription [[33:166|AIM 2-3-9a3]]. Teach the AIM colors.

AFH Chapter 2 says to test one brake, then the other [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]; the tailwheel chapter says to apply both brakes smoothly [[24:288|AFH 14-2]]. Application: either finds a weak brake if done gently right after moving; follow the POH if it says more.

AFH Chapter 2 gives elevator DOWN in any quartering tailwind [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]; the tailwheel chapter says that in light winds prop wash may make back stick more useful [[24:288|AFH 14-2]]. Teach the Chapter 2 rule first and the nuance at the tailwheel transition.

The AFH line 'if takeoff plans change while taxiing, recalculate the takeoff data' is in its jet chapter [[24:321|AFH 16-12]], so this lesson uses AC 91-73B instead, which is written for single-pilot Part 91 flying and flight schools and puts calculating takeoff data with the heads-down tasks done while stopped [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]]. Redoing the numbers for a piston single after a runway change is application.
AC 91-73B asks flight schools to have instructors limit cockpit instruction while taxiing [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3 para 2]]. Teach in the briefing and at the run-up area, not between hold lines.
AC 91-73B and the PHAK say 'Notices to Airmen'; the ACS says 'Notices to Air Missions'. It is the same NOTAM system.

AFH Figure 2-13 is a minimum set of hand signals; the AFH says the important thing is that each operation uses an agreed-upon set [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]. Ask the FBO what they use before a lesson at a marshaled ramp.

Runway incursion definitions, written clearances, hot spot briefings and LAHSO are in AI.II.C and CA.II.D. On the checkride, cross-reference rather than reteach them when the evaluator picks this Task.
gaps: The POH/AFM gives the taxi checklist, landing and taxi light duty limits, nosewheel steering limits and brake system details; the sources do not.
No source gives a number for taxi speed; the standard is 'stoppable by closing the throttle'.
No source describes how to judge the hold line position from the seat; that is CFI technique and is labeled application here.
AC 120-57 (low visibility SMGCS) and AC 00-34 (ramp signals) are referenced but not included, so low visibility taxi chart symbols and the full signal set are not covered.
Current hot spot descriptions and Chart Supplement entries for real airports must come from current publications.

activities.title: True or false: references and taxi instructions
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The Chart Supplement lists data such as hours of operation, fuel and lighting codes that a chart cannot show.
Airport diagrams are designed for use during approach and landing.
cards.why: False. They assist ground movement and are not intended for approach, landing or departure [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide, Airport Diagrams]].

cards.s: A closed taxiway will always be marked with a yellow X.
cards.why: False. A visual indication may not be present; check NOTAMs and ATIS [[33:161|AIM 2-3-6e]].

cards.s: When calling for taxi, always state your position on the airport.
A taxi clearance makes ATC responsible for avoiding collisions on the ground.
cards.why: False. It remains the pilot's responsibility to avoid collision with other aircraft [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b]].

cards.s: To acknowledge a light signal in daylight, move the ailerons or rudder.

activities.title: Read the sign array
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin. You are approaching the intersection from the bottom of the drawing.

pins.label: The taxiway you are on now
Turn here to go left at 90 degrees
Turn here to go right at 90 degrees

activities.title: Can I taxi beyond it?
activities.intro: Tap each item, then the bucket that says what the pavement beyond it means for the pilot.
buckets: Only with an ATC clearance (towered airport)

items.t: Broken double yellow edge lines beside an apron
Two solid yellow edge lines with a paved shoulder beyond
Yellow stripes painted across a taxiway shoulder
A taxiway entrance with a yellow cross on it
Two solid yellow lines on your side of a four-line marking at a runway
A single dashed line across the taxiway after ATC said 'hold short of Taxiway Bravo'
A single dashed line across the taxiway when ATC gave no hold instruction

activities.title: Work the numbers on the ramp
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You taxi on heading 090 with the wind from 140. How many degrees right of the nose is the wind?
items.why: 140 - 90 = 50 degrees right: a right quartering headwind, so right aileron up and elevator neutral [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

items.q: Heading 030, wind from 330. How many degrees left of the nose is the wind?
items.why: 30 - 330 = -300; -300 + 360 = 60 degrees left: a left quartering headwind [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

items.q: Heading 200, wind from 050. How many degrees left of the nose is the wind?
items.why: 200 - 50 = 150 degrees left: left rear, a quartering tailwind, so left aileron down (yoke right) and elevator down (yoke forward) [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

items.q: A runway centerline has a magnetic azimuth of 264 degrees. What runway number is painted on it?
items.why: The whole number nearest one-tenth of 264 is 26.4, rounded to 26 [[33:139|AIM 2-3-3b]].

items.q: Dashed taxiway edge markings use 15-foot lines with 25-foot gaps. How many lines start in 400 feet?
items.why: One line plus one gap is 15 + 25 = 40 feet; 400 / 40 = 10 [[33:145|AIM 2-3-4c2]].

items.q: Your Chart Supplement was issued 20 days ago. How many days until the next one?

activities.title: A learner's first night taxi, one decision at a time
activities.intro: Your learner has 25 hours and has never taxied at night. You are at your home towered field.

steps.s: Before you get in, what do you have the learner do?
options: Only check the landing light
Turn each light on briefly, tap the position light fixtures and walk the ramp with a flashlight
Start the engine and check lights from inside
Nothing extra; night preflight is the same as day
steps.why: Lights are checked by turning them on, position lights tapped for loose connections, and the ramp checked with a flashlight [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

steps.s: Which task do you keep for yourself on this first night taxi?
options: Steering
None; the learner does everything
The radio, so the learner can concentrate on night cues and control
The brake check
steps.why: Tasks should be done reasonably well in isolation before they are combined [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

steps.s: The learner keeps the landing light on all the way at slow speed. What do you mention?
options: Use the taxi light only on runways
Some landing lights overheat or drain the battery, and it may blind others
Turn on the strobes instead
Nothing; it is required
steps.why: Continuous landing light use may overheat it or drain the electrical system, and consider not blinding others [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

steps.s: Approaching the run-up area the learner is unsure whether she is on Bravo or Charlie. What is correct?
options: Keep going and look for a sign
Stop, but not on a runway, and ask ground
Ask for the tower frequency
Turn around on the taxiway
steps.why: If uncertain of position, never stop on a runway; stop and advise ATC, requesting progressive taxi if needed [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]].

steps.s: During the run-up, what is the night-specific risk to brief?
options: Carburetor ice
The airplane creeping forward unnoticed
Vapor lock
A dead battery
steps.why: At night the airplane can creep forward unnoticed; hold or lock the brakes and watch for movement [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

activities.title: Runway changed: put the redo in order
activities.intro: Ground has just changed your departure runway. Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Stop the airplane clear of runways if you are not sure where the new route goes
Read back the runway and any hold short with the call sign
Trace the new route and its hot spots on the diagram
Reset the control positions for the new legs and taxi
At the runway, set the heading bug and give the takeoff briefing again
Before adding power, confirm heading and runway agree
